title: Ὀδυσσεὺς καὶ Ναυσικάα
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Athena wakes Odysseus by a stratagem: a ball thrown at an attendant misses and falls into the river, the girls cry out, and he wakes on the bank. Naked and battered by the sea, he wonders what people live here, breaks off a leafy branch to cover himself, and comes out like a hungry lion. The girls flee; only Nausicaa, given courage by Athena, stands her ground, and he decides to plead from a distance rather than clasp her knees. His speech is flattery and appeal together: she is a goddess or a mortal three times blessed, he has been twenty days at sea, and he asks for the city and a rag to wear, wishing her a husband and a home of one mind. Nausicaa answers that Zeus deals out fortune, promises clothing and the name of her people, calls back her attendants, and orders them to feed and bathe the stranger. Odysseus, ashamed to be naked among the girls, asks them to stand apart.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ἄρ’ ἔμελλε πάλιν οἶκόνδε νέεσθαι
ζεύξασ’ ἡμιόνους πτύξασά τε εἵματα καλά,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē ar’ emelle palin oikonde neesthai
zeuxas’ hēmionous ptyxasa te heimata kala,
sentences.l:
But when now then she was about back homeward to go,
having yoked the mules and folded the fine clothes,
sentences.i: But when she was on the point of going back home, with the mules yoked and the fine clothes folded,
sentences.n: The scene is the river-bank, and Nausicaa (not named here) is packing up. ἔμελλε with an infinitive means 'was about to', and νέεσθαι is the present infinitive of νέομαι 'go back', uncontracted; οἶκόνδε is 'homeward', with the direction-suffix -δε. ζεύξασ’ and πτύξασά are aorist participles, 'having yoked' and 'having folded'. The sentence stays open until ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ in the next line, where the main clause begins.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
ὡς Ὀδυσεὺς ἔγροιτο, ἴδοι τ’ ἐυώπιδα κούρην,
ἥ οἱ Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν πόλιν ἡγήσαιτο.
sentences.tr:
enth’ aut’ all’ enoēse thea, glaukōpis Athēnē,
hōs Odyseus egroito, idoi t’ eyōpida kourēn,
hē hoi Phaiēkōn andrōn polin hēgēsaito.
sentences.l:
Then again another thing devised the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena,
that Odysseus might awake, and see the fair-eyed maiden,
who for him of the Phaeacian men the city would lead.
sentences.i: Then, in her turn, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, thought of something else: that Odysseus should wake and see the fair-eyed maiden, who would lead him to the city of the Phaeacians.
sentences.n: The first line is a formula and keeps the English it has where it stands elsewhere in the poem: Athena's 'other thing' is a further plan. ἔγροιτο, ἴδοι and ἡγήσαιτο are aorist optatives in a purpose clause after a past tense: 'that he might wake, and see, and that she might lead'. ἐυώπιδα is ἐυῶπις 'fair-eyed' (ἐύ- 'fair' and ὄψ 'eye'), kept apart from γλαυκῶπις 'gleaming-eyed'. ἥ οἱ: ἥ is the relative 'who', and οἱ is 'for him' (Homer's pronoun). The middle ἡγήσαιτο means 'lead the way', here with πόλιν as its goal.

sentences.t: σφαῖραν ἔπειτ’ ἔρριψε μετ’ ἀμφίπολον βασίλεια·
sentences.tr: sphairan epeit’ erripse met’ amphipolon basileia·
sentences.l: A ball then she threw at an attendant, the princess;
sentences.i: Then the princess threw a ball at one of her attendants;
sentences.n: This is the stratagem announced in 112–114. ἔρριψε is 'threw' (augmented, with the ρ doubled), and μετά with the accusative ἀμφίπολον means 'at, in the direction of'. ἀμφίπολος is 'attendant'. βασίλεια is the feminine of βασιλεύς 'king', so 'princess': Nausicaa, the king's daughter, standing alone at the end of the line.

sentences.t: ἀμφιπόλου μὲν ἅμαρτε, βαθείῃ δ’ ἔμβαλε δίνῃ·
sentences.tr: amphipolou men hamarte, batheiēi d’ embale dinēi·
sentences.l: The attendant she missed, and into a deep eddy she cast it;
sentences.i: She missed the attendant and threw the ball into a deep eddy;
sentences.n: ἁμαρτάνω takes the genitive, so ἀμφιπόλου μὲν ἅμαρτε is 'she missed the attendant'; ἅμαρτε is unaugmented (Attic ἥμαρτε), and so is ἔμβαλε (= ἐνέβαλε) 'threw into'. δίνη is a whirl or eddy of water, and βαθείῃ is the feminine dative of βαθύς 'deep'. The μέν … δέ pair sets the miss against the splash.

sentences.t: αἱ δ’ ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἄυσαν·
sentences.tr: hai d’ epi makron aysan·
sentences.l: and they, to a great distance, cried out;
sentences.i: and the girls gave a great cry that carried far;
sentences.n: The cry is the point of the stratagem, for it wakes him in the next words. ἐπὶ μακρόν is 'to a distance, far', and ἄυσαν is the aorist of ἀΰω 'shout', unaugmented. αἱ is 'they', the attendants: Homer's article-forms are often pronouns.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἔγρετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἑζόμενος δ’ ὥρμαινε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ egreto dios Odysseus,
hezomenos d’ hōrmaine kata phrena kai kata thymon·
sentences.l:
and he woke, heavenly Odysseus,
and sitting up he pondered in mind and in heart:
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus woke, and sitting up he pondered in his mind and heart:
sentences.n: ὁ is 'he' (a pronoun, not the article), and ἔγρετο is the aorist middle of ἐγείρω, 'he woke'. ἑζόμενος is the present participle of ἕζομαι 'sit', here 'sitting up', and ὥρμαινε is the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω 'turn over in the mind'. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν is a fixed phrase and keeps one English wherever it occurs. The · introduces his words; Murray prints no quotation marks.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι ἐγώ, τέων αὖτε βροτῶν ἐς γαῖαν ἱκάνω;
sentences.tr: ō moi egō, teōn aute brotōn es gaian hikanō;
sentences.l: “Oh me, I — of what mortals, this time, to the land do I come?
sentences.i: “Oh me! To the land of what mortals have I come this time?
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to himself, and his questions run on to 125. ὤ μοι ἐγώ is a cry of dismay, 'oh me!', with ἐγώ part of the cry. τέων is the epic genitive plural of τίς (Attic τίνων), ἐς is εἰς, and ἱκάνω is 'I arrive at'. αὖτε is 'again, this time'.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥ’ οἵ γ’ ὑβρισταί τε καὶ ἄγριοι οὐδὲ δίκαιοι,
ἦε φιλόξεινοι καί σφιν νόος ἐστὶ θεουδής;
sentences.tr:
ē rh’ hoi g’ hybristai te kai agrioi oude dikaioi,
ēe philoxeinoi kai sphin noos esti theoudēs;
sentences.l:
Is it that they are violent and savage and not just,
or hospitable, and to them the mind is god-fearing?
sentences.i: Are they violent and savage and unjust, or kind to strangers, with a god-fearing mind?
sentences.n: The first pair of alternatives. ἦ ῥ’ is the question-particle 'can it be that …?', a different word from the ἦ ῥα καὶ 'so she spoke' of 198. οἵ γ’ is 'they' (pronoun). ὑβρισταί are men of ὕβρις, overbearing violence; φιλόξεινοι is 'guest-loving' (φίλος and ξένος), and θεουδής 'god-fearing' (from θεός and δέος 'fear'). σφιν is the dative 'to them', and ἦε is 'or'.

sentences.t: ὥς τέ με κουράων ἀμφήλυθε θῆλυς ἀυτή·
sentences.tr: hōs te me kouraōn amphēlythe thēlys aytē·
sentences.l: As of maidens has come around me a female cry;
sentences.i: A cry as of girls, a woman’s shout, has come around me;
sentences.n: ὥς τέ introduces a comparison, 'as of'. κουράων is the genitive plural of κούρη 'girl', in -άων (Attic -ῶν). ἀμφήλυθε is 'has come around' (ἀμφί and ἦλθον, epic ἤλυθον), and ἀυτή is 'cry, shout'; θῆλυς 'female' agrees with it. The shout he heard at 117 is what he is trying to explain.

sentences.t:
νυμφάων, αἳ ἔχουσ’ ὀρέων αἰπεινὰ κάρηνα
καὶ πηγὰς ποταμῶν καὶ πίσεα ποιήεντα.
sentences.tr:
nymphaōn, hai echous’ oreōn aipeina karēna
kai pēgas potamōn kai pisea poiēenta.
sentences.l:
of nymphs, who hold the mountains’ steep peaks
and the springs of rivers and the grassy meadows.
sentences.i: of nymphs, who hold the steep peaks of the mountains, the springs of rivers, and grassy water-meadows.
sentences.n: νυμφάων is in apposition to κουράων: the 'girls' he imagines are nymphs (again the ending -άων for -ῶν). αἳ ἔχουσ’ is 'who hold', with αἵ the relative. κάρηνα, 'heads', are the peaks, the plural of κάρηνον, and πίσεα are water-meadows, low ground beside water. ποιήεντα 'grassy' is from ποίη 'grass'.

sentences.t: ἦ νύ που ἀνθρώπων εἰμὶ σχεδὸν αὐδηέντων;
sentences.tr: ē ny pou anthrōpōn eimi schedon audēentōn;
sentences.l: Can it be that I am, perhaps, near men endowed with speech?
sentences.i: Or am I, perhaps, somewhere near men speaking with human voices?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a fresh question, 'or can it be …?', and νύ που means 'now, perhaps'. αὐδηέντων is the genitive plural of αὐδήεις 'endowed with speech', and σχεδόν 'near' takes the genitive ἀνθρώπων: men, as against the nymphs he has just imagined. The exact force of αὐδήεις is debated; the English follows the ancient explanation 'having human speech'.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἐγὼν αὐτὸς πειρήσομαι ἠδὲ ἴδωμαι.
sentences.tr: all’ ag’ egōn autos peirēsomai ēde idōmai.
sentences.l: But come, I myself will make trial, and let me see.”
sentences.i: But come, I shall try for myself, and see.”
sentences.n: πειρήσομαι is the future 'I shall make trial', and ἴδωμαι is the aorist subjunctive 'let me see'; ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ 'but come!' introduces both. ἐγών is ἐγώ with an added -ν, and ἠδέ is 'and'. The self-address ends with the line.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν θάμνων ὑπεδύσετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἐκ πυκινῆς δ’ ὕλης πτόρθον κλάσε χειρὶ παχείῃ
φύλλων, ὡς ῥύσαιτο περὶ χροῒ μήδεα φωτός.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn thamnōn hypedyseto dios Odysseus,
ek pykinēs d’ hylēs ptorthon klase cheiri pacheiēi
phyllōn, hōs rhysaito peri chroï mēdea phōtos.
sentences.i: Having said this, heavenly Odysseus came out from under the thickets and broke off from the dense wood a leafy shoot with his stout hand, to cover his genitals.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is 'so having spoken'. ὑπεδύσετο is from ὑποδύομαι 'slip out from under', with θάμνων, 'thickets', in the genitive of separation. κλάσε is 'broke', unaugmented. πτόρθος is a shoot, and φύλλων 'of leaves' makes it a leafy one; παχείῃ is the feminine dative of παχύς 'thick, stout'. ῥύσαιτο is the aorist optative of ῥύομαι 'shield', after ὡς 'so that'; χροΐ is the uncontracted dative of χρώς 'skin'. μήδεα here is a different word from μήδεα 'counsels': it means 'genitals'.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ὥς τε λέων ὀρεσίτροφος ἀλκὶ πεποιθώς,
ὅς τ’ εἶσ’ ὑόμενος καὶ ἀήμενος, ἐν δέ οἱ ὄσσε
δαίεται·
sentences.tr:
bē d’ imen hōs te leōn oresitrophos alki pepoithōs,
hos t’ eis’ hyomenos kai aēmenos, en de hoi osse
daietai·
sentences.i: He went like a mountain-nurtured lion, trusting in his strength, that goes on through rain and wind with his eyes ablaze;
sentences.n: The lion simile begins. βῆ δ’ ἴμεν 'he set out to go' is the standing phrase for setting off, and βῆ is unaugmented (Attic ἔβη). ὥς τε introduces the simile, and the epic τε in ὅς τ’ marks what is true of lions in general. ὀρεσίτροφος is 'mountain-nurtured' and ἀλκί is the dative of ἀλκή 'defensive strength'. εἶσι is 'goes' (εἶμι), and ὑόμενος 'rained on' (ὕω) and ἀήμενος 'blown on' (ἄημι) are passive participles. ὄσσε is the dual 'the two eyes', with a singular verb.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ βουσὶ μετέρχεται ἢ ὀίεσσιν
ἠὲ μετ’ ἀγροτέρας ἐλάφους·
sentences.tr:
autar ho bousi meterchetai ē oiessin
ēe met’ agroteras elaphous·
sentences.l:
and he goes among cattle or sheep,
or after wild deer;
sentences.i: and he goes in among cattle or sheep, or after wild deer;
sentences.n: ὁ is 'he', the lion. μετέρχεται takes the dative here, 'goes among' (βουσί 'cattle', ὀίεσσιν 'sheep', datives in -σι and -εσσιν), and then μετ’ with the accusative means 'after': ἀγροτέρας ἐλάφους, 'wild deer' (ἀγρότερος 'of the fields, wild').

sentences.t:
κέλεται δέ ἑ γαστὴρ
μήλων πειρήσοντα καὶ ἐς πυκινὸν δόμον ἐλθεῖν·
sentences.tr:
keletai de he gastēr
mēlōn peirēsonta kai es pykinon domon elthein·
sentences.l:
and bids him, his belly,
to make trial of the flocks, and to go even into a solid house;
sentences.i: and his belly bids him make trial of the flocks and go even into a solid house;
sentences.n: κέλεται is 'bids, urges', and ἑ is the accusative 'him' (enclitic), so 'his belly bids him'. πειρήσοντα is a future participle, 'to try', with the genitive μήλων 'of the flocks' (μῆλα, sheep and goats). ἐλθεῖν is the aorist infinitive 'to go'. πυκινός is 'dense, close-packed': 'dense' of the wood at 128, but here, of a house, 'solid'.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ὀδυσεὺς κούρῃσιν ἐυπλοκάμοισιν ἔμελλε
μίξεσθαι, γυμνός περ ἐών·
sentences.tr:
hōs Odyseus kourēisin eyplokamoisin emelle
mixesthai, gymnos per eōn·
sentences.l:
So Odysseus among the fine-plaited girls was about
to mingle, naked though he was;
sentences.i: So Odysseus was about to mingle with the fine-plaited girls, naked though he was;
sentences.n: ὣς … ἔμελλε closes the simile: as the lion, so Odysseus. μίξεσθαι is 'to mix with, join the company of' (μίγνυμι), here simply 'to meet'. γυμνός περ ἐών is 'naked though he was', with concessive περ. Ὀδυσεύς with one σ is the same name as Ὀδυσσεύς (117, 127); the spelling follows the metre. ἐυπλοκάμοισιν 'fine-plaited' is the dative of ἐυπλόκαμος, here said of girls.

sentences.t: χρειὼ γὰρ ἵκανε.
sentences.tr: chreiō gar hikane.
sentences.l: for need had come.
sentences.i: for need had come upon him.
sentences.n: χρειώ is epic for χρεία 'need', and ἵκανε is the imperfect of ἱκάνω 'come upon', which the English renders 'had come upon (him)' because the clause gives a reason. The clause gives the reason for a naked man going among girls: necessity.

sentences.t:
σμερδαλέος δ’ αὐτῇσι φάνη κεκακωμένος ἅλμῃ,
τρέσσαν δ’ ἄλλυδις ἄλλη ἐπ’ ἠιόνας προὐχούσας·
sentences.tr:
smerdaleos d’ autēisi phanē kekakōmenos halmēi,
tressan d’ allydis allē ep’ ēionas prouchousas·
sentences.l:
Dreadful to them he appeared, ravaged by brine,
and they fled in fear, one this way, one that, over the jutting beaches;
sentences.i: He appeared to them a dreadful sight, battered by the brine, and they fled in fear, one this way and one that, along the jutting beaches;
sentences.n: σμερδαλέος 'dreadful to see' is predicative: 'he appeared dreadful'. αὐτῇσι is the feminine plural dative 'to them' (-ῃσι), and φάνη is the unaugmented aorist passive of φαίνομαι. κεκακωμένος is the perfect passive participle of κακόω 'ill-treat, ravage', and ἅλμῃ 'by the brine' is a dative of cause. τρέσσαν is the aorist third plural of τρέω 'flee in fear' (= ἔτρεσαν, unaugmented, with -σσ-), ἄλλυδις ἄλλη 'one one way, one another', and προὐχούσας 'jutting out'.

sentences.t: οἴη δ’ Ἀλκινόου θυγάτηρ μένε·
sentences.tr: oiē d’ Alkinoou thygatēr mene·
sentences.l: Alone the daughter of Alcinous stayed;
sentences.i: Alone, the daughter of Alcinous stood her ground;
sentences.n: οἴη is 'alone' (the feminine of οἶος), set against the flight of all the others in 138. μένε is the unaugmented imperfect 'stayed, held firm'. Nausicaa is called only 'the daughter of Alcinous' here; she is not named in this part until 186.

sentences.t:
τῇ γὰρ Ἀθήνη
θάρσος ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε καὶ ἐκ δέος εἵλετο γυίων.
sentences.tr:
tēi gar Athēnē
tharsos eni phresi thēke kai ek deos heileto guiōn.
sentences.l:
for to her Athena
courage in her mind put, and fear from her limbs took away.
sentences.i: for Athena had put courage in her mind and taken the fear from her limbs.
sentences.n: τῇ is the dative of the pronoun, 'to her' (Homer's article-forms are pronouns), and the line says why she alone stood firm: Athena's plan of 112–114 goes on. θῆκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι. ἐκ … εἵλετο is tmesis, 'took out', with δέος 'fear' and γυίων 'from her limbs' (γυῖα, in the genitive of separation). ἐνὶ φρεσί is 'in her mind'.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἄντα σχομένη·
sentences.tr: stē d’ anta schomenē·
sentences.l: and she stood, facing him, holding firm;
sentences.i: and she stood there facing him and held her ground;
sentences.n: στῆ is unaugmented (Attic ἔστη). ἄντα is an adverb, 'face to face, in front', and σχομένη is the aorist middle participle of ἔχω, 'holding herself, checking herself'. The unit stops at the · in mid-line, and ὁ δέ 'but he' turns to Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ὁ δὲ μερμήριξεν Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἢ γούνων λίσσοιτο λαβὼν ἐυώπιδα κούρην,
ἦ αὔτως ἐπέεσσιν ἀποσταδὰ μειλιχίοισι
λίσσοιτ’, εἰ δείξειε πόλιν καὶ εἵματα δοίη.
sentences.tr:
ho de mermērixen Odysseus,
ē gounōn lissoito labōn eyōpida kourēn,
ē autōs epeessin apostada meilichioisi
lissoit’, ei deixeie polin kai heimata doiē.
sentences.l:
and he pondered, Odysseus,
whether by the knees to beseech, having taken hold of the fair-eyed maiden,
or just with words, standing apart, gentle,
to beseech, in case she might show the city and give clothes.
sentences.i: and Odysseus wavered whether to clasp the knees of the fair-eyed maiden and beseech her, or to beg her with gentle words from a distance, in the hope that she would show him the city and give him clothes.
sentences.n: μερμήριξεν 'was in two minds, pondered' is followed by two alternatives, ἢ … ἦ, 'whether … or' (the second is printed ἦ but means 'or'). λίσσοιτο is an optative of deliberation after a past tense, 'whether to beseech'. To clasp the knees was the suppliant's ritual gesture (γούνων is the genitive after λαβών, 'having taken hold of'). ἀποσταδά 'standing apart', αὔτως 'just so, merely', and μειλιχίοισι 'gentle': the phrase ἐπέεσσιν ἀποσταδὰ μειλιχίοισι recurs word for word at 146, and so does its English. εἰ … δείξειε … δοίη is 'in case she might show … and give', with εἰ and the optative expressing a hope.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα οἱ φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι,
λίσσεσθαι ἐπέεσσιν ἀποσταδὰ μειλιχίοισι,
μή οἱ γοῦνα λαβόντι χολώσαιτο φρένα κούρη.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara hoi phroneonti doassato kerdion einai,
lissesthai epeessin apostada meilichioisi,
mē hoi gouna labonti cholōsaito phrena kourē.
sentences.l:
So then, to him as he considered, it seemed better to be,
to beseech with words, standing apart, gentle,
lest to him having taken her knees she might be angered in mind, the maiden.
sentences.i: So, as he weighed it, this seemed to him the better course, to plead with gentle words from a distance, lest the girl be angered in her heart if he clasped her knees.
sentences.n: The first line stands word for word in an earlier part and keeps its English there. δοάσσατο is an epic aorist, 'it seemed', and φρονέοντι 'as he considered' is a dative agreeing with οἱ. κέρδιον is the comparative of κέρδος 'gain': 'more advantageous, better'. The second half is a fear clause, μή … χολώσαιτο, an optative after a past tense, 'lest she be angered' (φρένα 'in mind' is an accusative of respect). οἱ … λαβόντι is 'to him having clasped', a dative of the person concerned, and γοῦνα is the epic accusative plural 'knees'.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα μειλίχιον καὶ κερδαλέον φάτο μῦθον.
sentences.tr: autika meilichion kai kerdaleon phato mython.
sentences.l: Straightway gentle and cunning he spoke a speech.
sentences.i: At once he spoke a gentle and cunning speech:
sentences.n: φάτο is the unaugmented past tense of φημί 'spoke'. μειλίχιος 'gentle' and κερδαλέος 'cunning' (from κέρδος 'gain') stand side by side: the speech that follows is gentle in manner and shrewd in aim, and both adjectives keep the same English wherever they occur. The full stop closes the sentence and the speech follows in the next unit; Murray prints it without quotation marks.

sentences.t: γουνοῦμαί σε, ἄνασσα·
sentences.tr: gounoumai se, anassa·
sentences.l: “I beseech you at your knees, queen;
sentences.i: “I entreat you, queen:
sentences.n: The speech opens with the formal appeal of a suppliant. γουνοῦμαι is made from γόνυ 'knee': 'I supplicate at your knees'. Odysseus has just decided not to touch them (145–147), so here the knee is only in the verb. ἄνασσα is 'queen', the address to a lady of rank or to a goddess.

sentences.t: θεός νύ τις, ἦ βροτός ἐσσι;
sentences.tr: theos ny tis, ē brotos essi;
sentences.l: a god, then, some, or a mortal are you?
sentences.i: are you some god, or a mortal?
sentences.n: The question sets two possibilities, and the speech takes them in turn: the god at 150–152, the mortal at 153–159. θεός νύ τις, ἦ βροτός ἐσσι: ἦ is 'or' here, τις 'some', and ἐσσι the epic second person of εἰμί, 'you are'.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν τις θεός ἐσσι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσιν,
Ἀρτέμιδί σε ἐγώ γε, Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο,
εἶδός τε μέγεθός τε φυήν τ’ ἄγχιστα ἐίσκω·
sentences.tr:
ei men tis theos essi, toi ouranon euryn echousin,
Artemidi se egō ge, Dios kourēi megaloio,
eidos te megethos te phyēn t’ anchista eiskō·
sentences.i: If you are one of the gods who hold the wide heaven, then it is to Artemis, daughter of great Zeus, that I liken you most nearly, in form, in size and in stature;
sentences.n: εἰ μέν τις θεός ἐσσι opens the first branch, 'if you are a god'; τοί is the relative 'who' (= οἵ), and ἔχουσιν 'hold'. Ἀρτέμιδι is the dative of the thing compared, with ἐίσκω 'liken' and ἄγχιστα 'nearest'. The accusatives εἶδος, μέγεθος and φυήν say in what respect: 'form, size, stature'.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τίς ἐσσι βροτῶν, τοὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ ναιετάουσιν,
τρὶς μάκαρες μὲν σοί γε πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ,
τρὶς μάκαρες δὲ κασίγνητοι·
sentences.tr:
ei de tis essi brotōn, toi epi chthoni naietaousin,
tris makares men soi ge patēr kai potnia mētēr,
tris makares de kasignētoi·
sentences.i: But if you are one of the mortals who live on the earth, three times blessed are your father and your lady mother, three times blessed your brothers;
sentences.n: εἰ δέ τίς ἐσσι βροτῶν opens the second branch, 'if you are a mortal'. ναιετάουσιν is uncontracted for Attic ναιετῶσι, 'dwell'. τρὶς μάκαρες is 'three times blessed', with μάκαρ the word usually used of the gods; πότνια μήτηρ is 'lady mother' (πότνια 'lady, mistress', the title of a woman of rank), and κασίγνητοι are 'brothers'.

sentences.t:
μάλα πού σφισι θυμὸς
αἰὲν ἐυφροσύνῃσιν ἰαίνεται εἵνεκα σεῖο,
λευσσόντων τοιόνδε θάλος χορὸν εἰσοιχνεῦσαν.
sentences.tr:
mala pou sphisi thymos
aien eyphrosynēisin iainetai heineka seio,
leussontōn toionde thalos choron eisoichneusan.
sentences.l:
very surely for them the heart
always with gladness is warmed for your sake,
as they look on such a shoot entering the dance.
sentences.i: Surely their hearts are always warmed with gladness on your account, as they look on so fine a young shoot entering the dance.
sentences.n: μάλα πού is 'surely, I suppose'. σφισι is the pronoun 'to them'; θυμός is 'heart' here, and ἰαίνεται 'is warmed, cheered'. εἵνεκα σεῖο is 'for your sake' (σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ). λευσσόντων is a genitive participle, 'as they look on'. θάλος 'shoot, young growth' is a neuter noun, but the participle εἰσοιχνεῦσαν 'entering' agreeing with it is feminine, because it is the girl who is meant.

sentences.t:
κεῖνος δ’ αὖ περὶ κῆρι μακάρτατος ἔξοχον ἄλλων,
ὅς κέ σ’ ἐέδνοισι βρίσας οἶκόνδ’ ἀγάγηται.
sentences.tr:
keinos d’ au peri kēri makartatos exochon allōn,
hos ke s’ eednoisi brisas oikond’ agagētai.
sentences.l:
And that man in turn, exceedingly in heart, most blessed beyond others,
who, having outweighed you with bridal gifts, shall lead you home.
sentences.i: And he, beyond all others, is the most blessed of heart, who outweighs his rivals with bridal gifts and leads you to his home.
sentences.n: κεῖνος is 'that man' (Ionic for ἐκεῖνος). περί is here an adverb, 'exceedingly', with κῆρι 'in the heart'; μακάρτατος is 'most blessed', and ἔξοχον ἄλλων 'beyond all others'. βρίσας is the aorist participle of βρίθω 'be heavy, weigh down'; its object is σε, so the Greek says literally 'having outweighed you with bridal gifts' (as in l), and 'outweighs his rivals' in the English is an interpretation: the suitor whose gifts weigh most. ἐέδνοισι are 'bridal gifts', those given by the suitor. ἀγάγηται is a middle subjunctive with κε, 'shall lead (as his own)', and οἶκόνδε is 'homeward' with -δε.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω τοιοῦτον ἴδον βροτὸν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
οὔτ’ ἄνδρ’ οὔτε γυναῖκα·
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō toiouton idon broton ophthalmoisin,
out’ andr’ oute gynaika·
sentences.l:
For never yet such a mortal have I seen with my eyes,
neither man nor woman;
sentences.i: For I have never yet seen such a mortal with my own eyes, neither man nor woman;
sentences.n: The praise turns to wonder. οὐ … πω is 'not yet', ἴδον is unaugmented (Attic εἶδον), and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is a dative plural, 'with my eyes'. The pair οὔτε … οὔτε says that no man and no woman he has seen looked like this.

sentences.t: σέβας μ’ ἔχει εἰσορόωντα.
sentences.tr: sebas m’ echei eisoroōnta.
sentences.l: awe holds me, looking on you.
sentences.i: Awe takes hold of me as I look at you.
sentences.n: σέβας is 'awe, reverence'. εἰσορόωντα is the participle of εἰσοράω 'look at', uncontracted, agreeing with μ’ (με): 'me looking at you'.

sentences.t:
Δήλῳ δή ποτε τοῖον Ἀπόλλωνος παρὰ βωμῷ
φοίνικος νέον ἔρνος ἀνερχόμενον ἐνόησα·
sentences.tr:
Dēlōi dē pote toion Apollōnos para bōmōi
phoinikos neon ernos anerchomenon enoēsa·
sentences.l:
At Delos once such a one, beside Apollo’s altar,
a palm-tree’s young shoot rising up, I noticed;
sentences.i: At Delos once, beside the altar of Apollo, I noticed just such a young shoot of a palm tree growing up;
sentences.n: Δήλῳ is 'at Delos', the island of Apollo, and the altar is his. φοῖνιξ is 'palm-tree' (the same word can also mean 'purple' and 'Phoenician'). ἔρνος is a young shoot, and ἀνερχόμενον 'springing up'. τοῖον 'such' says the sapling was of the same kind as she is; the comparison is spelled out at 167–168, where the sapling is the standard of wonder. ἐνόησα is 'I noticed, took note of'.

sentences.t:
ἦλθον γὰρ καὶ κεῖσε, πολὺς δέ μοι ἕσπετο λαός,
τὴν ὁδὸν ᾗ δὴ μέλλεν ἐμοὶ κακὰ κήδε’ ἔσεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ēlthon gar kai keise, polys de moi hespeto laos,
tēn hodon hēi dē mellen emoi kaka kēde’ esesthai.
sentences.l:
For I went there too, and a great host followed me,
on the journey on which evil sorrows were to be for me.
sentences.i: For I went there too, with a great host following me, on the journey on which evil sorrows were to be mine.
sentences.n: The aside tells how he came to see the palm: he went to Delos too, with many followers. ἦλθον γὰρ καὶ κεῖσε is 'for I went there too' (κεῖσε 'thither'). ἕσπετο is the aorist of ἕπομαι 'follow' (Attic ἑσπόμην). τὴν ὁδὸν ᾗ is 'the journey on which', and μέλλεν … ἔσεσθαι, from μέλλω with the future infinitive, means 'was destined to be'. κακὰ κήδεα are 'evil sorrows'.

sentences.t:
ὣς δ’ αὔτως καὶ κεῖνο ἰδὼν ἐτεθήπεα θυμῷ
δήν, ἐπεὶ οὔ πω τοῖον ἀνήλυθεν ἐκ δόρυ γαίης,
ὡς σέ, γύναι, ἄγαμαί τε τέθηπά τε, δείδια δ’ αἰνῶς
γούνων ἅψασθαι·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ autōs kai keino idōn etethēpea thymōi
dēn, epei ou pō toion anēlythen ek dory gaiēs,
hōs se, gynai, agamai te tethēpa te, deidia d’ ainōs
gounōn hapsasthai·
sentences.i: In just the same way, when I saw that, I was long amazed in my heart, for never yet had such a trunk come up from the earth as you, lady, whom I marvel at and am amazed by, and I am terribly afraid to clasp your knees;
sentences.n: The comparison is completed: as he wondered at the palm, so at her. ὣς δ’ αὔτως is 'just in the same way'. ἐτεθήπεα is the pluperfect of τέθηπα 'be astonished', used as a past tense; δήν is 'for long'. ἀνήλυθεν is the aorist 'came up' (epic ἤλυθον), which the English puts in the pluperfect after ἐτεθήπεα. δόρυ is 'wood, timber, trunk' (also 'spear'), here the trunk of the palm. ὡς σέ is 'as (I wonder at) you'. ἄγαμαι is 'admire', and δείδια 'I fear' is a perfect with present sense. γούνων ἅψασθαι is 'to touch your knees' (ἅπτομαι takes the genitive), the suppliant's gesture again.

sentences.t: χαλεπὸν δέ με πένθος ἱκάνει.
sentences.tr: chalepon de me penthos hikanei.
sentences.l: and harsh grief comes upon me.
sentences.i: and a harsh grief has come over me.
sentences.n: χαλεπὸν … πένθος is 'harsh grief', the subject, with με the object of ἱκάνει 'comes upon'. The next lines tell what has caused it.

sentences.t: χθιζὸς ἐεικοστῷ φύγον ἤματι οἴνοπα πόντον·
sentences.tr: chthizos eeikostōi phygon ēmati oinopa ponton·
sentences.l: Yesterday, on the twentieth day, I escaped the wine-faced open-sea;
sentences.i: Yesterday, on the twentieth day, I escaped the sea that has the look of wine;
sentences.n: χθιζός is an adjective 'of yesterday' used like an adverb. ἐεικοστῷ ἤματι is 'on the twentieth day' (ἐεικοστός is the epic form of εἰκοστός). φύγον is unaugmented (Attic ἔφυγον). οἴνοπα is the accusative of οἶνοψ, 'having the look of wine' (οἶνος and ὄψ), the standing epithet of the sea, translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δέ μ’ αἰεὶ κῦμ’ ἐφόρει κραιπναί τε θύελλαι
νήσου ἀπ’ Ὠγυγίης.
sentences.tr:
tophra de m’ aiei kym’ ephorei kraipnai te thyellai
nēsou ap’ Ōgygiēs.
sentences.l:
and all that while the wave ever bore me, and rushing storm-blasts,
from the island of Ogygia.
sentences.i: and all that time the wave carried me on, and the rushing storm-blasts, from the island of Ogygia.
sentences.n: τόφρα is 'meanwhile, all that time'. ἐφόρει is the imperfect of φορέω 'carry, keep carrying', with κῦμ’ 'the wave' as subject and κραιπναὶ … θύελλαι 'rushing storm-blasts' joined to it. Ὠγυγίης is the Ionic genitive of Ὠγυγίη 'Ogygia', the island he has come from, and νήσου ἀπ’ is 'from the island'. The unit ends mid-line at the full stop.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐνθάδε κάββαλε δαίμων,
ὄφρ’ ἔτι που καὶ τῇδε πάθω κακόν·
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ enthade kabbale daimōn,
ophr’ eti pou kai tēide pathō kakon·
sentences.l:
But now here a power cast me down,
so that still, perhaps, here too I may suffer evil;
sentences.i: And now some power has cast me down here, so that even here, I suppose, I may still suffer further evil;
sentences.n: κάββαλε is κατά + βάλε: κατά loses its final vowel and the τ is assimilated to the following β, and the verb has no augment (= κατέβαλε). δαίμων is 'a divine power', not a god known by name. ὄφρ’ … πάθω is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive of πάσχω, 'so that I may suffer', said bitterly, as if the power's aim were more suffering. τῇδε is 'here'.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὀίω
παύσεσθ’, ἀλλ’ ἔτι πολλὰ θεοὶ τελέουσι πάροιθεν.
sentences.tr:
ou gar oiō
pausesth’, all’ eti polla theoi teleousi paroithen.
sentences.l:
for I do not think it will cease,
but still many things the gods will bring to pass before that.
sentences.i: for I do not think it will stop; the gods will first bring many more things to pass.
sentences.n: ὀίω 'I think, suppose' takes the future infinitive παύσεσθ’ (παύσεσθαι, elided) 'that it will cease', with 'my sufferings' understood as the subject. τελέουσι is the future of τελέω 'accomplish', uncontracted. πάροιθεν is 'before (that), first'.

sentences.t: ἀλλά, ἄνασσ’, ἐλέαιρε·
sentences.tr: alla, anass’, eleaire·
sentences.l: But, queen, have pity;
sentences.i: But, queen, take pity on me;
sentences.n: ἐλέαιρε is the present imperative of ἐλεαίρω 'pity'. The vocative ἄνασσ’ (elided) is again 'queen'. The plea is bare; its reason follows at once.

sentences.t:
σὲ γὰρ κακὰ πολλὰ μογήσας
ἐς πρώτην ἱκόμην, τῶν δ’ ἄλλων οὔ τινα οἶδα
ἀνθρώπων, οἳ τήνδε πόλιν καὶ γαῖαν ἔχουσιν.
sentences.tr:
se gar kaka polla mogēsas
es prōtēn hikomēn, tōn d’ allōn ou tina oida
anthrōpōn, hoi tēnde polin kai gaian echousin.
sentences.i: for after toiling through many evils I have come to you first, and of the others who hold this city and land I know no one.
sentences.n: σὲ γὰρ κακὰ πολλὰ μογήσας ἐς πρώτην ἱκόμην means 'you are the first I have come to after toiling through many evils'; ἐς πρώτην 'to the first' agrees with σέ. μογήσας is the aorist participle of μογέω 'toil, labour hard'. οὔ τινα … ἀνθρώπων is 'no one of men', a partitive genitive, and οἳ … ἔχουσιν 'who hold' the city, with τήνδε 'this'.

sentences.t:
ἄστυ δέ μοι δεῖξον, δὸς δὲ ῥάκος ἀμφιβαλέσθαι,
εἴ τί που εἴλυμα σπείρων ἔχες ἐνθάδ’ ἰοῦσα.
sentences.tr:
asty de moi deixon, dos de rhakos amphibalesthai,
ei ti pou eilyma speirōn eches enthad’ iousa.
sentences.l:
The city to me show, and give a rag to throw around me,
if you had any wrapper for the cloths, coming here.
sentences.i: Show me the city, and give me a rag to throw around me, if you had any wrapper for the cloths when you came here.
sentences.n: δεῖξον and δός are aorist imperatives, and ἀμφιβαλέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive 'to throw around oneself', giving ῥάκος 'rag' its purpose. εἴλυμα is a wrapper, covering, and σπείρων is the genitive plural of σπεῖρον 'cloth'; the exact sense of εἴλυμα σπείρων is not certain, and 'a wrapper for the cloths' is the simplest reading (the clothes folded at 111 are what he means). ἔχες is the unaugmented imperfect (Attic εἶχες), and ἰοῦσα the participle of εἶμι 'go, come'.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δὲ θεοὶ τόσα δοῖεν ὅσα φρεσὶ σῇσι μενοινᾷς,
ἄνδρα τε καὶ οἶκον, καὶ ὁμοφροσύνην ὀπάσειαν
ἐσθλήν·
sentences.tr:
soi de theoi tosa doien hosa phresi sēisi menoināis,
andra te kai oikon, kai homophrosynēn opaseian
esthlēn·
sentences.i: And may the gods give you all that your own heart desires, a husband and a home, and may they grant you good accord of mind;
sentences.n: σοὶ δὲ θεοὶ τόσα δοῖεν ὅσα … is a wish: δοῖεν is the aorist optative of δίδωμι, 'may they give', and τόσα … ὅσα is 'as many as'. σῇσι is the possessive σός with the epic dative ending -ῃσι, agreeing with φρεσί ('in your own mind', from φρήν), and μενοινᾷς is 'you desire' (μενοινάω). ὁμοφροσύνη is 'oneness of mind', and ὀπάσειαν is an aorist optative of ὀπάζω 'grant'. ἐσθλήν 'good' opens the next line, carried over from ὁμοφροσύνην.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γὰρ τοῦ γε κρεῖσσον καὶ ἄρειον,
ἢ ὅθ’ ὁμοφρονέοντε νοήμασιν οἶκον ἔχητον
ἀνὴρ ἠδὲ γυνή·
sentences.tr:
ou men gar tou ge kreisson kai areion,
ē hoth’ homophroneonte noēmasin oikon echēton
anēr ēde gynē·
sentences.i: For truly nothing is stronger or better than this: when husband and wife keep house, of one mind in their thoughts;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ is 'for truly not', and τοῦ γε is 'than this'; κρεῖσσον and ἄρειον are comparatives, 'stronger, better' and 'better', with 'there is' understood. ὅθ’ is ὅτε 'when'. ὁμοφρονέοντε is a dual participle (uncontracted) and ἔχητον a dual subjunctive: the two people, husband and wife, are the subject. νοήμασιν is 'in their thoughts'.

sentences.t:
πόλλ’ ἄλγεα δυσμενέεσσι,
χάρματα δ’ εὐμενέτῃσι, μάλιστα δέ τ’ ἔκλυον αὐτοί.
sentences.tr:
poll’ algea dysmeneessi,
charmata d’ eumenetēisi, malista de t’ eklyon autoi.
sentences.l:
many pains to their enemies,
and joys to their well-wishers, and most of all they themselves have heard it.”
sentences.i: much pain to those who wish them ill, joy to those who wish them well, and they themselves know it best.”
sentences.n: The line has no verb; supply 'there are'. δυσμενέεσσι is the dative of δυσμενής 'ill-disposed, hostile', in -εσσι, and εὐμενέτῃσι the dative of εὐμενέτης 'well-wisher', in -ῃσι. ἔκλυον is an aorist 'they have heard', used for general truth (as is the epic τε in τ’); the sense of μάλιστα δέ τ’ ἔκλυον αὐτοί is not quite certain, and the English follows the reading that the couple themselves know it best.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Ναυσικάα λευκώλενος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Nausikaa leukōlenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn white-armed Nausicaa spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then white-armed Nausicaa spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is a reply-formula of the same pattern as the one for Telemachus, with the epithet λευκώλενος 'white-armed'. ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak', ἀντίον 'face to face'. Nausicaa is named here for the first time in this part. She now answers the stranger; Murray prints no quotation marks.

sentences.t: ξεῖν’, ἐπεὶ οὔτε κακῷ οὔτ’ ἄφρονι φωτὶ ἔοικας·
sentences.tr: xein’, epei oute kakōi out’ aphroni phōti eoikas·
sentences.l: “Stranger, since neither to a bad nor to a foolish man do you look like;
sentences.i: “Stranger, since you look like neither a bad man nor a foolish one —
sentences.n: ξεῖν’ (ξεῖνε, elided) is 'stranger', the ordinary address to a guest or a man from another country. The ἐπεί clause is not completed by a main clause: she turns to Zeus at once, and comes back to the point with a fresh ἐπεί at 191. κακῷ and ἄφρονι agree with φωτί (φώς 'man'): 'neither a bad nor a senseless man'. ἔοικας 'you look like, you seem' takes the dative.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δ’ αὐτὸς νέμει ὄλβον Ὀλύμπιος ἀνθρώποισιν,
ἐσθλοῖς ἠδὲ κακοῖσιν, ὅπως ἐθέλῃσιν, ἑκάστῳ·
sentences.tr:
Zeus d’ autos nemei olbon Olympios anthrōpoisin,
esthlois ēde kakoisin, hopōs ethelēisin, hekastōi·
sentences.l:
Zeus himself dispenses prosperity, the Olympian, to men,
to good and to bad, however he may wish, to each one;
sentences.i: it is Zeus himself, the Olympian, who dispenses prosperity to men, to the good and to the bad, as he may wish, to each one;
sentences.n: ὄλβος is 'prosperity, good fortune'. νέμει is 'dispenses, distributes', and Ὀλύμπιος 'the Olympian'. ἐσθλοῖς ἠδὲ κακοῖσιν is 'to the good and to the bad' (datives plural), ὅπως ἐθέλῃσιν 'however he may wish' (a subjunctive with no κε), and ἑκάστῳ 'to each'. It is her answer to the stranger's complaint at 173–174: Zeus gives as he pleases.

sentences.t: καί που σοὶ τάδ’ ἔδωκε, σὲ δὲ χρὴ τετλάμεν ἔμπης.
sentences.tr: kai pou soi tad’ edōke, se de chrē tetlamen empēs.
sentences.l: And perhaps to you he has given these things, and you must endure them all the same.
sentences.i: And perhaps he has given you these things, and you must endure them all the same.
sentences.n: καί που is 'and perhaps'. τάδε 'these things' are his sufferings. τετλάμεν is the perfect infinitive of τλῆναι 'endure', the root of πολύτλας; χρή 'it is necessary'; ἔμπης 'all the same, in any case'. The line draws the practical moral: he must bear it.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’, ἐπεὶ ἡμετέρην τε πόλιν καὶ γαῖαν ἱκάνεις,
οὔτ’ οὖν ἐσθῆτος δευήσεαι οὔτε τευ ἄλλου,
ὧν ἐπέοιχ’ ἱκέτην ταλαπείριον ἀντιάσαντα.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’, epei hēmeterēn te polin kai gaian hikaneis,
out’ oun esthētos deuēseai oute teu allou,
hōn epeoich’ hiketēn talapeirion antiasanta.
sentences.l:
But now, since to our city and land you have come,
neither of clothing will you be in want, nor of anything else,
of which it is fitting that a much-tried suppliant, meeting us, should have.
sentences.i: But now, since you have come to our city and land, you will lack neither clothing nor anything else that is fitting for a suppliant so much tried to have when he meets with us.
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ is 'but as things are'. δευήσεαι is the uncontracted future of δεύομαι 'lack, be in need of', with the genitive: ἐσθῆτος 'clothing' and τευ (= τινος) 'anything'. ὧν … ἀντιάσαντα: ὧν 'of which' is genitive after ἀντιάω 'meet with, come by', so 'the things a suppliant should get when he comes upon us'; ἐπέοιχ’ (ἐπέοικε) is 'it is fitting'. ταλαπείριος 'much-tried' (τλάω and πεῖρα 'trial') agrees with ἱκέτην 'suppliant'.

sentences.t: ἄστυ δέ τοι δείξω, ἐρέω δέ τοι οὔνομα λαῶν.
sentences.tr: asty de toi deixō, ereō de toi ounoma laōn.
sentences.l: And the city to you I shall show, and I shall tell you the name of the people.
sentences.i: I will show you the city, and tell you the name of its people.
sentences.n: τοι is the enclitic dative 'to you' (= σοι), not the particle. δείξω and ἐρέω are futures, 'I shall show' and 'I shall tell' (ἐρέω = Attic ἐρῶ). οὔνομα is ὄνομα 'name', and λαῶν 'of the people' means the Phaeacians she is about to name.

sentences.t:
Φαίηκες μὲν τήνδε πόλιν καὶ γαῖαν ἔχουσιν,
εἰμὶ δ’ ἐγὼ θυγάτηρ μεγαλήτορος Ἀλκινόοιο,
τοῦ δ’ ἐκ Φαιήκων ἔχεται κάρτος τε βίη τε.
sentences.tr:
Phaiēkes men tēnde polin kai gaian echousin,
eimi d’ egō thygatēr megalētoros Alkinooio,
tou d’ ek Phaiēkōn echetai kartos te biē te.
sentences.l:
The Phaeacians hold this city and land,
and I am the daughter of great-spirited Alcinous,
and on him, of the Phaeacians, depends the might and the force.”
sentences.i: The Phaeacians hold this city and land, and I am the daughter of great-spirited Alcinous, and on him depends the might and force of the Phaeacians.”
sentences.n: Φαίηκες are the Phaeacians, and ἔχουσιν 'hold' repeats the verb of 177. μεγαλήτορος is 'great-spirited' (the same epithet and the same line-end as when she is named at 213). τοῦ δ’ ἐκ … ἔχεται is 'and on him hangs', from ἔχομαι 'cling, depend'; κάρτος τε βίη τε 'might and force' are the subject, with Φαιήκων 'of the Phaeacians' between. She gives her identity by her father, not by her own name.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀμφιπόλοισιν ἐυπλοκάμοισι κέλευσε·
sentences.tr: ē rha kai amphipoloisin eyplokamoisi keleuse·
sentences.l: She spoke, and to her attendants, fine-plaited, gave orders:
sentences.i: So she said, and gave orders to her fine-plaited attendants:
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα is the formula 'so she spoke' (from ἠμί 'say'); it is not the ἦ ῥ’ of 120, which is a question-particle. καί adds a second act: 'and she gave orders to'. ἐυπλοκάμοισι 'fine-plaited' (ἐύ- and πλόκαμος 'braid, lock') is a dative plural, and κέλευσε 'ordered' takes the dative. Her orders to the attendants follow, again without quotation marks in the Greek.

sentences.t: στῆτέ μοι, ἀμφίπολοι·
sentences.tr: stēte moi, amphipoloi·
sentences.l: “Stand, for me, attendants;
sentences.i: “Stop, attendants;
sentences.n: στῆτε is the aorist imperative of ἵστημι, 'stop!', with μοι 'for me' as a dative of interest. ἀμφίπολοι 'attendants' is the vocative. What she stops is their flight of 138.

sentences.t: πόσε φεύγετε φῶτα ἰδοῦσαι;
sentences.tr: pose pheugete phōta idousai;
sentences.l: whither do you flee, having seen a man?
sentences.i: where are you running, at the sight of a man?
sentences.n: πόσε is 'to where?' (the epic form of ποῖ). φῶτα ἰδοῦσαι is 'having seen a man' (φώς 'man'; ἰδοῦσαι the aorist participle, feminine plural). The question is a rebuke: they flee merely 'at seeing a man'.

sentences.t: ἦ μή πού τινα δυσμενέων φάσθ’ ἔμμεναι ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.tr: ē mē pou tina dysmeneōn phasth’ emmenai andrōn;
sentences.l: Surely you do not say that he is one of hostile men?
sentences.i: Surely you do not think he is one of our enemies?
sentences.n: ἦ μή πού … is a question that expects the answer 'no'. φάσθ’ is φάσθε, the second plural of φημί 'say, think'. ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (= Attic εἶναι). δυσμενέων ἀνδρῶν is 'of hostile men' (δυσμενής 'ill-disposed'), a partitive genitive after τινα: 'one of the enemy men'.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἔσθ’ οὗτος ἀνὴρ διερὸς βροτὸς οὐδὲ γένηται,
ὅς κεν Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν ἐς γαῖαν ἵκηται
δηιοτῆτα φέρων·
sentences.tr:
ouk esth’ houtos anēr dieros brotos oude genētai,
hos ken Phaiēkōn andrōn es gaian hikētai
dēiotēta pherōn·
sentences.i: There is no such man, no living mortal, nor ever will be, who comes to the land of the Phaeacians bringing war;
sentences.n: οὐκ ἔσθ’ οὗτος ἀνήρ is 'there is no such man'. The meaning of διερός is uncertain: 'living' is the traditional guess, and 'wet' and 'lively' have also been proposed; the English follows the first. οὐδὲ γένηται is 'nor will there ever be' (an aorist subjunctive of γίγνομαι with the sense of a future). ὅς κεν … ἵκηται is a general relative clause, 'who comes', and ἐς is εἰς. δηιοτής is 'hostile encounter, battle', and φέρων 'bringing'. The unit stops at the · in mid-line.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ φίλοι ἀθανάτοισιν.
sentences.tr: mala gar philoi athanatoisin.
sentences.l: for very dear are we to the immortals.
sentences.i: for we are very dear to the immortals.
sentences.n: φίλοι is passive here, 'dear (to)', and takes the dative ἀθανάτοισιν 'to the immortals'; 'we are' is understood. This is her reason for the claim just made.

sentences.t:
οἰκέομεν δ’ ἀπάνευθε πολυκλύστῳ ἐνὶ πόντῳ,
ἔσχατοι, οὐδέ τις ἄμμι βροτῶν ἐπιμίσγεται ἄλλος.
sentences.tr:
oikeomen d’ apaneuthe polyklystōi eni pontōi,
eschatoi, oude tis ammi brotōn epimisgetai allos.
sentences.l:
We dwell apart in the much-washed open-sea,
the farthest, and none other of mortals mingles with us.
sentences.i: We live far apart in the wave-washed sea, the farthest of men, and no other mortal has dealings with us.
sentences.n: οἰκέομεν is the uncontracted οἰκοῦμεν 'we dwell', and ἀπάνευθε 'far apart'. πολυκλύστῳ is 'much washed by waves' (πολυ- and κλύζω 'wash, dash'). ἔσχατοι is 'farthest' (of all peoples), and ἄμμι is the epic form of ἡμῖν 'to us'; ἐπιμίσγεται is 'mingles, has dealings with'. The isolation is the reason no enemy can come.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅδε τις δύστηνος ἀλώμενος ἐνθάδ’ ἱκάνει,
τὸν νῦν χρὴ κομέειν·
sentences.tr:
all’ hode tis dystēnos alōmenos enthad’ hikanei,
ton nyn chrē komeein·
sentences.l:
But this one, some wretched man, wandering, here has come,
him now it is necessary to tend;
sentences.i: But this is some wretched wanderer who has come here, and him we must now look after;
sentences.n: ὅδε τις is 'this one here, someone'. δύστηνος is 'wretched, unlucky', and ἀλώμενος 'wandering' (ἀλάομαι); ἱκάνει 'has come' is a present that describes the arrival. χρή is 'it is necessary', and κομέειν is the uncontracted infinitive of κομέω 'tend, look after'; τὸν is the pronoun 'him'. The unit breaks at the · in mid-line.

sentences.t:
πρὸς γὰρ Διός εἰσιν ἅπαντες
ξεῖνοί τε πτωχοί τε, δόσις δ’ ὀλίγη τε φίλη τε.
sentences.tr:
pros gar Dios eisin hapantes
xeinoi te ptōchoi te, dosis d’ oligē te philē te.
sentences.l:
for from Zeus are all
strangers and beggars, and a gift is small and dear.
sentences.i: for all strangers and beggars are from Zeus, and a small gift is welcome.
sentences.n: πρὸς Διός εἰσιν means 'are from Zeus' (πρός with the genitive, 'from, under the protection of'): strangers and beggars are in Zeus's care, which is why the man must be fed. ξεῖνοί τε πτωχοί τε is 'strangers and beggars'. δόσις is 'gift', and ὀλίγη τε φίλη τε 'small and dear', φίλη here meaning 'welcome'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ δότ’, ἀμφίπολοι, ξείνῳ βρῶσίν τε πόσιν τε,
λούσατέ τ’ ἐν ποταμῷ, ὅθ’ ἐπὶ σκέπας ἔστ’ ἀνέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
alla dot’, amphipoloi, xeinōi brōsin te posin te,
lousate t’ en potamōi, hoth’ epi skepas est’ anemoio.
sentences.l:
But give, attendants, to the stranger both food and drink,
and bathe him in the river, where there is shelter from the wind.”
sentences.i: So give the stranger food and drink, attendants, and bathe him in the river, where there is shelter from the wind.”
sentences.n: δότ’ (δότε) and λούσατε are aorist imperatives, 'give' and 'bathe (him)'. ξείνῳ is the Ionic form of ξένῳ (ξεῖνος), 'to the stranger'. βρῶσις 'food' and πόσις 'drink' are nouns of action. ὅθ’ is ὅθι 'where', ἔστ’ 'there is', and σκέπας ἀνέμοιο 'shelter from the wind' (σκέπας 'covering, shelter'). Her orders close the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, αἱ δ’ ἔσταν τε καὶ ἀλλήλῃσι κέλευσαν,
κὰδ δ’ ἄρ’ Ὀδυσσῆ’ εἷσαν ἐπὶ σκέπας, ὡς ἐκέλευσεν
Ναυσικάα θυγάτηρ μεγαλήτορος Ἀλκινόοιο·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hai d’ estan te kai allēlēisi keleusan,
kad d’ ar’ Odyssē’ heisan epi skepas, hōs ekeleusen
Nausikaa thygatēr megalētoros Alkinooio·
sentences.i: So she spoke, and they stopped and urged one another on, and sat Odysseus down in the shelter, as Nausicaa, daughter of great-spirited Alcinous, had ordered;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is 'so she spoke' (ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο, elided). ἔσταν is the aorist third plural of ἵστημι in its intransitive sense, 'they stopped' (= ἔστησαν), and ἀλλήλῃσι is 'to one another' (feminine dative plural in -ῃσι). κὰδ … εἷσαν is tmesis, 'they seated', with κάδ for κατά (the τ assimilated to δ). Ὀδυσσῆ’ is the elided accusative Ὀδυσσῆα. σκέπας is the wind-shelter of 210. The last line stands word for word in an earlier part and keeps its English there.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δ’ ἄρα οἱ φᾶρός τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματ’ ἔθηκαν,
δῶκαν δὲ χρυσέῃ ἐν ληκύθῳ ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον,
ἤνωγον δ’ ἄρα μιν λοῦσθαι ποταμοῖο ῥοῇσιν.
sentences.tr:
par d’ ara hoi pharos te chitōna te heimat’ ethēkan,
dōkan de chryseēi en lēkythōi hygron elaion,
ēnōgon d’ ara min lousthai potamoio rhoēisin.
sentences.l:
And beside him a cloak and a tunic, clothes, they put,
and gave, in a golden flask, liquid oil,
and bade him bathe in the streams of the river.
sentences.i: They laid beside him a cloak and a tunic, clothes for him, and gave him liquid oil in a golden flask, and told him to bathe in the streams of the river.
sentences.n: πὰρ is παρά; with οἱ 'beside him' and ἔθηκαν 'they put'. φᾶρος is a man's cloak here, χιτών a tunic, and εἵματα 'garments' stands in apposition to both. δῶκαν is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι, 'they gave'. λήκυθος is an oil-flask, and ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον is 'liquid oil', the oil he will use at 219–220. ἤνωγον 'they bade' belongs to ἄνωγα, a perfect with present sense; λοῦσθαι is 'to bathe', and ῥοῇσιν the dative plural 'streams'.

sentences.t: δή ῥα τότ’ ἀμφιπόλοισι μετηύδα δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: dē rha tot’ amphipoloisi metēuda dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: Then indeed among the attendants spoke heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then heavenly Odysseus spoke among the attendants:
sentences.n: δή ῥα τότ’ is 'then indeed, at that moment'. μετηύδα is 'spoke among' (the imperfect of μεταυδάω), and δῖος is 'heavenly'. The line introduces Odysseus's last speech in this part; the Greek has no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ἀμφίπολοι, στῆθ’ οὕτω ἀπόπροθεν, ὄφρ’ ἐγὼ αὐτὸς
ἅλμην ὤμοιιν ἀπολούσομαι, ἀμφὶ δ’ ἐλαίῳ
χρίσομαι·
sentences.tr:
amphipoloi, stēth’ houtō apoprothen, ophr’ egō autos
halmēn ōmoiin apolousomai, amphi d’ elaiōi
chrisomai·
sentences.i: “Attendants, stand off at that distance, so that I myself may wash the brine from my shoulders and anoint myself with oil;
sentences.n: στῆθ’ (στῆτε) is the imperative 'stand', οὕτω 'just so', and ἀπόπροθεν 'far off': he asks them to keep their distance. ὄφρ’ … ἀπολούσομαι is ὄφρα with a future indicative, 'so that I may wash off'. ὤμοιιν is a dual, 'from my two shoulders', and ἅλμη is 'brine'. ἀμφὶ … χρίσομαι is tmesis, 'I shall anoint (myself) all over', and ἐλαίῳ is 'with oil'. The unit stops at the · in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἦ γὰρ δηρὸν ἀπὸ χροός ἐστιν ἀλοιφή.
sentences.tr: ē gar dēron apo chroos estin aloiphē.
sentences.l: for indeed for a long time from my skin oil has been away.
sentences.i: for it is a long time since there was oil on my skin.
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is 'for truly'. ἀπὸ χροός is 'away from the skin' (χρώς, genitive χροός), and ἐστιν … ἀλοιφή 'there is oil': the sentence says literally 'oil is long away from my skin'. δηρόν is 'for a long time' and ἀλοιφή 'oil, ointment, grease'.

sentences.t: ἄντην δ’ οὐκ ἂν ἐγώ γε λοέσσομαι·
sentences.tr: antēn d’ ouk an egō ge loessomai·
sentences.l: But face to face I will not bathe;
sentences.i: But I will not bathe in front of you;
sentences.n: ἄντην is an adverb, 'face to face, openly', and λοέσσομαι is the future of λούω 'bathe'. οὐκ ἂν … λοέσσομαι: ἄν with a future is unusual, and the sense is plain refusal. γε is 'at least'.

sentences.t:
αἰδέομαι γὰρ
γυμνοῦσθαι κούρῃσιν ἐυπλοκάμοισι μετελθών.
sentences.tr:
aideomai gar
gymnousthai kourēisin eyplokamoisi metelthōn.
sentences.l:
for I am ashamed
to be stripped, having come among fine-plaited girls.”
sentences.i: for I am ashamed to be naked among the fine-plaited girls.”
sentences.n: αἰδέομαι is 'I am ashamed' (from αἰδώς 'shame, reverence'), with the infinitive γυμνοῦσθαι 'to be stripped, to go naked' (from γυμνός). μετελθών is 'having come among', with the dative κούρῃσιν. His reason is modesty: he will not bathe before the girls. The phrase κούρῃσιν ἐυπλοκάμοισι is the same as at 135.
